habitat: Groups of three to ten in thornveld and mixed bushveld, preferring lightly wooded, well-grassed country, hunting from a perch on a bush.
summary: A common resident. A distinctive long-tailed pied bird. Both sexes have a white wing-stripe. The female may show white on the flanks and has a shorter tail. The immature is bronze-brown with a grey rump. The call is prooit-preeoo, prooit-preeoo-preeoo, the first sound descending and the second ascending. From a distance Newman says it can be mistaken for a long-tailed widowbird or a whydah. The Kemp code RB, under the paper name Longtailed Shrike, was left unchanged.

similar.note: Pin-tailed Whydah can look long-tailed and pied at a distance. Magpie Shrike is a heavier bird with a white wing-stripe, in small groups.
Shaft-tailed Whydah is one of the long-tailed birds Newman names as a distant confusion.
Long-tailed Paradise Whydah is one of the long-tailed birds Newman names as a distant confusion.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman calls it a common resident. Pied parts are not split into black and white tokens where the text only says pied, apart from the white wing-stripe and the female’s white flanks. Long-tailed Widowbird and Broad-tailed Paradise-Whydah are named by Newman and are not in this list. Population figures and the Kemp code RB were left unchanged.
